skeptic.objection: The lead's grade A and its 'likely' entitlement path rest on a future land use of Industrial. The city's own authoritative record for its July 2025 Comprehensive Development Plan says the development-pattern layer replaced that future land use dataset, and on the parcel's own polygon that layer shows only Low Density Residential. So the Industrial value is superseded, and the adopted plan points to houses. The tract is also zoned R-4, and recorded single-family subdivisions touch it: The Villages at Oakshire Phase 2 along its north line and Forest Valley lots. Industrial use would need a plan amendment and a rezoning next to existing homes, and a residential-named owner may intend houses. A person must settle whether any such path is realistic before this is treated as an industrial lead.

claims.text: The city's own ArcGIS Online record for its development-pattern layer calls it the authoritative layer created by the Comprehensive Development Plan passed in July 2025, replacing the now-deprecated Future Land Use dataset. So the development pattern, not the old future land use value, is the adopted plan's designation.
claims.quote: The authoritative Development Patterns GIS layer created by the Comprehensive Development Plan passed in July 2025. The Development Patterns replaces the Future Land Use dataset, which is now deprecated.

The same record says the layer carries the previous Future Land Use fields alongside the development patterns, with the logic used to translate one into the other. This confirms the 'Industrial' value the screener used (LANDUSEDES) is the superseded field, not the adopted designation.
claims.quote: This layer contains both Development Patterns as well as previous Future Land Use fields. Additionally, it contains the Translation Logic, which was the way the Future Land Use was translated into the new Development Patterns.

claims.text: Queried with the parcel's own polygon (from the Fulton parcel layer), not a bounding box, the development-pattern layer returns exactly one feature, OBJECTID 16892: development pattern LDR (Low Density Residential), with the old field reading Industrial. Its SHAPE.AREA is 8,660,485 sq ft (about 199 acres); the ACRES value of 1,053 is a carried-over attribute, not this polygon's size.

The Fulton County subdivisions layer, queried with the parcel's polygon, returns one recorded subdivision touching the parcel: The Villages at Oakshire Phase 2 (recorded 2005, about 45.8 acres). The parcel sits beside a platted single-family subdivision; it is not inside it (see open items).

The City of Atlanta cadastral city-lots layer, queried with the parcel's polygon, returns platted house lots of The Villages at Oakshire Phase 2 (plat book 277, pages 55-57) touching the parcel. The query also returns about 21 such lots.

The same query also returns platted lots of Forest Valley Unit 2 (plat book 80, page 11) and Forest Valley Subdivision Unit 1 touching the parcel. Single-family subdivisions adjoin it on more than one side.

At a point inside the parcel (-84.3525, 33.6505) the city-lots layer returns one unplatted city lot (PIN 14 0001 LL060, about 35.8 GIS acres) with no plat name, book or page. No residential subdivision plat is recorded on the land itself in this layer.

The first pass's sewer claim names laterals on Erica Wy inside the bounding box. If confirmed, the north neighbour is a recently built subdivision, likely to oppose an industrial rezoning.

Is this tract an unbuilt later phase of the Oakshire development or of another residential plan? The owner's name contains 'Residential', and the last recorded sale (2011, $45,100 for 36.7 acres per the brief) looks like a distressed sale. A person should pull the deed and any preliminary plat or land-disturbance permit. No permit search was made: the city's permit portal is a search form.
